short: The application checks the cache, loads missing values from storage and fills the cache.
detail: On a miss, the caller reads the source, writes the result with a TTL and returns it. Updates need a separate policy.
design: Keep the database sized for cold starts and miss spikes. Even a high steady-state hit ratio can hide how much traffic the source receives after eviction.

short: A cache that loads a missing value through its own adapter.
detail: Callers always read from the cache API. On a miss, its loader fetches the value and populates the entry before returning it.
design: A shared loader centralizes timeouts, miss coordination and instrumentation. Give operators a plan for a loader or cache outage.

short: The rules that determine who writes each layer and when the application acknowledges a write.
detail: Invalidate-on-write and update-on-write commit the source first, then issue a separate cache command. With write-through or write-behind the write enters through the cache layer.
design: Choose the order against your durability and freshness requirements. Assign ownership for retries, ordering and recovery from partial writes.

short: A cache-mediated write that waits for the backing store before acknowledging.
detail: The cache layer synchronously writes the backing store. The simulator makes a new cache value visible after the source commits.
design: This centralizes write coordination and puts source write latency on the response path. Handle commit-then-timeout, cache publication failure and retry ordering explicitly.

short: A cache-mediated write that acknowledges before the backing store commits.
detail: The new value reaches the cache first. A background worker flushes pending writes, possibly batching or combining successive updates.
design: Decide what an acknowledgment promises. Use durable buffering and per-key ordering if acknowledged updates must survive a cache or worker crash.

short: Removing a cached entry so a later miss has to reload it.
detail: Invalidate-on-write deletes the cache key after the source commits. A delete has no memory of the version unless you also keep a version fence.
design: Track failed invalidations and bound staleness with a TTL. Where ordering matters, use monotonic versioned fills or a fence that survives the delete.

short: A response that uses an older version or a copy past its freshness limit.
detail: A cache can return an old value while its TTL is still running. This simulator also counts responses deliberately served past TTL during a grace period.
design: Define tolerated staleness by use case. A product description can often lag while authorization or an inventory reservation may require a stronger read.

short: An in-flight reader refills a cache with data from before a writer’s invalidation.
detail: A reader misses and takes the old database snapshot. A writer commits a new row and deletes the key. The delayed reader then fills the now-empty key with the old snapshot.
design: Deleting after commit still leaves a race with a prior read. If you need a freshness guarantee, retain a version fence or use monotonic versioned keys and reads.

short: How long a cached copy is considered fresh after a fill.
detail: At expiry a normal lookup misses. Stale-while-revalidate can retain the expired copy for a separate, bounded grace period.
design: Choose fresh time from the maximum tolerable stale interval and the expected reload load. Check how cache outage, expiry and rebuild affect the source.

short: The fraction of read lookups served directly from the cache.
detail: The simulator counts grace-period responses as hits and coalesced waiters as misses. It counts stale responses separately.
design: Look at the hit ratio by key family and pair it with source load and freshness. One very popular key can obscure misses elsewhere.

short: Database operations started over the last modeled second.
detail: The rate includes cache fills, refreshes and writes. In-flight counts describe concurrent work, and the peak records its high-water mark.
design: Observe both rate and concurrency. A short load spike can exhaust a connection pool while its minute-average QPS still looks normal.

short: Many callers try to reload the same missing cache entry at once.
detail: When a popular key expires, every caller that reaches it before the first fill may query the source. This is also called a thundering herd.
design: Coalesce reloads within the right scope and protect the source with a concurrency budget. Measure the worst expiry interval as well as the overall hit ratio.

short: Concurrent misses for the same key share one in-flight fetch.
detail: A leader fetches the result and followers wait for it. Singleflight usually coordinates within a process. Several app instances need a common coordinator for fleet-wide deduplication.
design: Set a deadline and release followers when a fetch fails. A distributed lease needs a bounded lifetime and may need fencing to prevent an expired owner from writing.

short: Serving an expired copy briefly while refreshing it in the background.
detail: The stale copy is eligible during a bounded grace interval. A refresh guard limits background reloads while the copy continues to serve requests.
design: Use a separate grace budget for data that can lag. Track refresh failures so you know when a cache is relying on expired copies.

short: A cache hit sometimes triggers a refresh before its copy expires.
detail: A hit draws an exponential random lead time and refreshes when that lead exceeds the remaining TTL. With more hits near expiry, a refresh has more opportunities to start.
design: Useful when hot keys have enough lead traffic to refresh ahead of demand. It spends extra database reads and still needs a fallback when no refresh finishes in time.

short: Random variation in the TTL of each new cache fill.
detail: The simulator draws each duration independently from 75% to 125% of the configured TTL. One entry still has one expiry shared by all callers.
design: Use jitter to spread bulk-loaded expiries. Pair it with per-key protection when the risk is a single hot key.

short: A limiter that saves unused capacity as tokens and spends one token per admitted request.
detail: The refill rate controls sustained admission. Capacity limits the stored credit, so a full bucket allows a burst up to that limit.
design: Choose burst capacity from the spike the downstream service can absorb. Idle clients can all spend their stored credit together.

short: A finite queue that releases requests at a steady pace.
detail: This simulator uses the queueing form. It accepts while slots are available, drains one request per interval and rejects once full.
design: Size the buffer from both the tolerated queue delay and expected burst. Adding capacity can trade fewer rejections for worse response tails.

short: A limiter that counts requests in aligned, non-overlapping time periods.
detail: Each boundary resets the counter. Two capacity-sized bursts just before and after a boundary can send twice the limit in a short span.
design: Use it when simple counters and low memory matter and the downstream can absorb boundary spikes. Define how clocks agree on the window across instances.

short: A quota over the most recent interval, measured from each new arrival.
detail: An exact rolling log trims old accepted timestamps and tests the number that remain. A weighted pair of fixed counters is a lower-memory approximation.
design: Use an exact window when a rolling hard cap matters. Budget timestamp storage and atomic trim-and-admit work per client.

short: The HTTP status for a request rejected because it exceeded a rate limit.
detail: A server can include Retry-After to suggest when to retry. Callers that retry together can create another spike.
design: Provide clients a recovery contract and monitor rejects by quota class. Separate deliberate throttling from backend errors when measuring availability.

short: The identity on which a rate limiter groups requests and charges quota.
detail: Typical keys include account IDs, credentials, IP addresses or a combination of identity and route. This simulator maintains separate limiter state for two clients.
design: Choose keys that match your fairness and abuse model. Shared IPs can group unrelated callers, and unlimited key cardinality can exhaust the limiter.

short: A cluster of arrivals close together compared with service or refill time.
detail: Bursts can exceed the instantaneous capacity of a system even when average arrivals over a longer interval are sustainable.
design: Model arrival shape as well as sustained rate. Decide which bursts to absorb with credit or queueing and where to reject excess load.

short: Admission lets a request into a system, and forwarding sends it on for work.
detail: The token and window policies forward immediately after admission here. Leaky bucket admits to a buffer and forwards later as each slot drains.
design: Measure admits, forwards and queue time separately. A high admit rate can hide work waiting in a shaping buffer.

short: How quickly the limiter earns a new token or releases a queued request.
detail: Token credit accrues continuously up to capacity. The leaky bucket schedules one departure at each configured interval while work waits.
design: Select a sustained rate the downstream can handle. Refill rate alone doesn’t determine the worst burst or maximum queue delay.

short: A placement scheme that moves a limited subset of keys when membership changes.
detail: On a ring, adding a node transfers ranges from the owners that previously covered them. Removing a node transfers just the ranges that node owned.
design: Useful for clients that need a stable, independently calculated placement. Coordinate membership updates, and plan for key migration if data is durable.

short: A circular ordering of key hashes and node positions.
detail: Keys belong to the first owner position clockwise. The last hash wraps around to the first position. Each position owns the preceding arc.
design: Every router needs the same hash, ring membership and tie-breaking rules. Otherwise two routers can send the same key to different owners.

short: A placement rule that picks the node at index hash(key) remainder N.
detail: With a fixed node list and uniform hash it spreads key counts evenly. Changing N changes the remainder for many keys and removal can also shift node indices.
design: Modulo works when partition count is stable. Use a fixed partition indirection if you need to add machines without remapping keys against a different divisor.

short: One of several ring positions owned by the same physical node.
detail: Each position owns a short random arc. Summing many arcs usually evens out the share per physical owner. Capacity weighting can assign more positions to larger nodes.
design: Changing position count itself remaps keys. Virtual nodes reduce random ownership skew while a single hot key still maps to one owner.

short: Changing which nodes own keys after a change in placement.
detail: With many evenly spread positions, adding one node to an N-node ring moves about 1/(N+1) of keys. Removing one moves the departing node’s share, about 1/N.
design: Measure the amount and demand of moved data. Cache owners may refill on demand, while durable owners need state transfer and an explicit cutover.

short: A key that accounts for unusually high traffic compared with other keys.
detail: It can dominate cache miss traffic or one physical node’s work, even with an even key distribution. Adding virtual nodes leaves each key with one owner.
design: Measure demand per key or group. Replicate safe reads, split the key when semantics permit, or isolate and cap the workload.

short: Key distribution counts owned keys, while traffic share weights them by requests.
detail: They agree when all keys have equal demand. A hot key can make traffic uneven even when physical nodes hold similar key counts.
design: Choose a balance metric that reflects the real bottleneck, such as requests, bytes or CPU. Verify key ownership and load separately.

short: A component that chooses a backend for each incoming unit of work.
detail: This replay compares per-request routing. A transport load balancer can instead choose per connection, which groups requests differently when a connection carries many.
design: Choose a routing unit and load signal that reflect the work. Health checks and routing should handle slow backends as well as hard failures.

short: The jobs waiting for a server’s limited service capacity.
detail: Each server here has one worker and serves jobs in arrival order. The outstanding count includes the job in service and all waiting jobs.
design: Bound backlog and track queue wait independently of service time. A service can look healthy on CPU or median latency while some queues build up.

short: The time a server spends doing the job after it reaches the head of the queue.
detail: The same request has the same underlying work across policy pools. The slow server takes five times longer for the same work in this model.
design: Measure service time apart from waiting. Identical queue depths can imply different delays on servers with different workloads or execution speeds.

short: Routing to each server in turn in a repeating order.
detail: Each complete rotation assigns one request to each server. The choice requires no outstanding count and gives degraded servers the same turn as healthy ones.
design: A predictable baseline for homogeneous backends and jobs. Weights or feedback are useful if capacity differs or changes.

short: Choosing a backend uniformly at random for every request.
detail: Independent routing balances in expectation. Several successive requests can hit one server even when other servers are idle.
design: Simple to run across independent balancers. Sampling a second server gives feedback on local imbalance without a full scan.

short: Routing to a server with the smallest count of pending requests or active connections.
detail: This simulator counts running and queued requests. Connection-based implementations count open connections, which can carry multiple requests or remain idle.
design: Select a signal that tracks actual work. If several balancers share counters, consider staleness and synchronized decisions when replicas see the same apparent minimum.

short: Compare two randomly sampled backends and pick the one with less work.
detail: The replay samples distinct servers and compares outstanding requests. This uses two counter reads per decision regardless of pool size, while a linear least-outstanding scan uses N.
design: A fleet can approximate the benefits of least connections or least outstanding without a global minimum. Stale or misleading local signals can still hurt.

short: p50 is the middle of the sample, while p99 is the boundary for its slowest roughly 1%.
detail: The simulator sorts completed arrivals and selects the nearest-rank observation. Durations include the modeled arrival hop, queue wait and service time.
design: Compare equal, fully completed cohorts. During a replay, slow requests can remain queued while fast completions make p99 look lower.
